article_text:
The competition in the art world for business in the Gulf is heating up. Next week Christie’s is set to host its first fine art auction in Abu Dhabi , featuring some 70 lots of modern and contemporary Middle Eastern art.

The sale, dubbed “ MAWASIM: 20 Years of Modern and Contemporary Middle Eastern Art,” features works by Turkish abstractionist Fahrelnissa Zeid, one of the first women to attend art school in Turkey; Iraqi painter Faisel Laibi Sahi; Egyptian modernist painter Mahmoud Saïd; and Palestinian American artist Samia Halaby, among others. Estimates for works in the sale range from $8,000–$12,000 to $500,000–$700,000. (Mawasim means “seasons” in Arabic and is meant to reference the 20 years since Christie’s held its first sale in the United Arab Emirates, in Dubai, in 2006.)

In an interview with the Khaleej Times , the house’s chairman for the Middle East and Africa, Ridha Moumni, called the sale “probably the most important event of modern and contemporary Eastern art for many years.”

The sale is something of a starting pistol for what is rapidly becoming the November arts season for the UAE: several weeks later, from November 19–22, Frieze will host the first edition of its Abu Dhabi fair at Manarat Al Saadiyat, and just a few weeks after that, on December 11, the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi will finally open its doors. And on December 10, Sotheby’s will culminate the second edition of its “Collectors’ Week” in the emirate with its i naugural fine art sale , titled “Breaking Ground,” to be hosted at the new Saadiyat Grove Experience Center on Saadiyat Island, the city’s cultural hub. (Sotheby’s sale, notably, features works with much higher top estimates and headline names like Andy Warhol and Claude Monet.)

There will be some major works featured by Christie’s in Abu Dhabi, though they won’t be for sale. Rather, the house has said it will be showing, starting Wednesday, three major works from its upcoming marquee New York sales: Wassily Kandinsky’s Betonte Ecken (1923), which carries a $60 million to $80 million estimate; Mark Rothko’s Untitled (1968), which carries a $10 million to $15 million estimate; and Pablo Picasso’s Tête de femme (1939), which carries a $12 million to $18 million estimate. All three works will be on view at Abu Dhabi Edition hotel on Al Bateen Marina.

One imagines that Christie’s is hoping those lots catch the eye of some deep-pocketed Gulf collectors ahead of the sales. After all, Moumni touted to the Times , “The UAE is the country where we have the biggest number of bidders in our auction. In terms of concentration, the UAE is the land of collectors of modern and contemporary art.”
excerpt_original: As Frieze, Sotheby's, and the Guggenheim descend on Abu Dhabi, Christie's will stage its first art auction in the emirate.

article_text:
Hélia Paukner will become the director of macLYON and the artistic director of the Lyon Biennale.

She takes over from Isabelle Bertolotti, who has held both positions since 2018.

Paukner arrives from Mucem – the Museum of European and Mediterranean Civilisations, a national museum of cultural anthropology in Marseille, where she has been curator and head of contemporary art since 2019. Her appointment marks a return to Lyon having previously served as research assistant to the director at the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon.

Paukner will oversee the appointment of the curator for each the art biennale, the eighteenth edition of which is open through 13 December, curated by Catherine Nichols. Paukner will also coordinate the staging of the Lyon Dance Biennale, which takes places on alternate years to the art event.

article_text:
For the first time, a Bob Ross painting will come to auction in Germany.

The painting comes to the block on December 5 at auctioneer Ketterer Kunst in Munich, from the collection of American Public Television (APT). Proceeds will benefit the organization as part of a charitable initiative dreamed up by Joan Kowalski, president of Bob Ross, Inc., to support public television stations in the US following cuts of $9 billion to previously approved government funding by a Republican-dominated Congress, at the behest of Donald Trump’s presidential administration.

Mountain Splendor (1986) bears an estimate of €40,000–€60,000 ($46,800–$70,200). Ross painted it live on television during season seven, episode eight in of his beloved show The Joy of Painting . Ross typically created three versions of his compositions, the auctioneer points out: one in preparation, one on live television, and one for his instructional books, with the live-painted ones the most coveted. The painting has been in storage for decades and emerges in “exceptionally well-preserved condition,” says Ketterer Kunst in press materials.

Mountain Splendor will be on show at the house’s showrooms in Frankfurt, Cologne, Hamburg, Berlin, and Munich between November 8 and December 4.

“Bob Ross has inspired millions of people to take up painting and has long since been an icon of pop culture,” says Robert Ketterer, owner and auctioneer. “With Mountain Splendor , we’re auctioning off a piece of television history. What makes it so special is the fact that people can still watch the artist create this painting today. The fact that we’re able to offer an original for the first time in Germany—and at the same time support public television in the U.S.—makes this auction particularly special to us.”

Ross’s paintings have sold for as much as $1 million at benefit auctions, when late-night comedian John Oliver last year sold Cabin at Sunset , painted for a 1986 episode.

As far as public auction houses listed on Artnet’s price database, Ross’s auction high stands at $787,900, achieved with the 1990 painting Change of Seasons at Bonhams Skinner in January against a $60,000 high estimate. The auctioneer raised some $1.3 million for APT that night with the sale of three Ross paintings, with the record painting going for more than thirteen times its high estimate. Last November, Bonhams brought three of a planned 30 of his canvases to auction; they sold for a total of $600,000, all of which went to APT.

One private seller is trying to smash even the $1 million high, with Minnesota art gallery Modern Artifact asking $9.85 million for A Walk in the Woods , painted on the show’s very first episode.

“Bob Ross is one of America’s most beloved cultural exports, and audiences across the globe love his work as much as viewers here in the States do,” said Jim Dunford, CEO and president of APT, in press materials. “These auctions turn that worldwide affection for Bob into real support for local public television stations, and we are deeply grateful to Bob Ross Inc. for making it possible.”

Indeed, Ross is a hit in Germany; his show debuted on German television in 2001 and continues to air regularly. Samsung TV Plus Germany also features the Bob Ross Channel auf Deutsch, which launched this year.

The American public, too, can’t get enough of Ross, whose show aired some 403 episodes and ran from 1983 to 1994. Comic actor Owen Wilson played a fictionalized version of him in the 2023 feature Paint (which Shanti Escalante-de Mattei, writing for ARTnews , called “a flaw-filled film”). His estate has been at the center of a legal battle, depicted in a 2021 Netflix documentary that the estate called “inaccurate and heavily slanted.”

article_text:
Alan Dysert , known best for his role as Sean Cudahy on All My Children , has died, his wife Michele Dysert revealed in a Facebook post Sunday. He was 75.

“My heart is broken as I share that my beloved husband, Alan, passed away on October 23, 2026, Michele Dysert wrote. “While I am struggling to imagine life without him, I am forever grateful to have experienced what so many people spend their lives searching for — the love of a lifetime.”

Related Stories

2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries

Walter Koenig Dies: ‘Star Trek’s Original Ensign Chekov Was 90

His wife did not reveal a cause of death but in his 2023 autobiography, Lights, Camera, Cancer!, Alan revealed that he had been diagnosed with a “rare, aggressive and incurable cancer.” According to the book’s synopsis, he’d undergone “four major cancer-related surgeries, one recurrence, many rounds of chemotherapy and 29 CT scans to date.”

Dysert appeared as Sean Cudahy in 79 episodes of All My Children, from 1980-1990, a character described as a devious yet humorous con man and villain, who contrasted sharply with his brother, good guy Tom Cudahy (played by Richard Shoberg).

He also worked on several movies, including Cheech and Chong’s Next Movie , and was an executive producer, co-exec producer or associate producer on films including The Grift, Becoming Jesse Tate, The Senator, My Many Sons , and just this year in The Legend of Van Dorn.

“Alan had an incredible gift for storytelling, a wonderful sense of humor, an adventurous spirit, and a personality that could fill any room,” Michele Dysert wrote. “His life was filled with remarkable experiences, fascinating people, and enough stories for several lifetimes. And he loved sharing them.”

You can read her entire post below.

My heart is broken as I share that my beloved husband, Alan, passed away on October 23, 2026. While I am struggling to imagine life without him, I am forever grateful to have experienced what so many people spend their lives searching for — the love of a lifetime. Alan lived an extraordinary life. From his humble beginnings as a farm boy in Illinois, he went on to become an actor, musician, writer, filmmaker, producer, and beloved acting teacher. Many knew him from his years on All My Children, while thousands of others knew him as the teacher and mentor who encouraged them to believe in themselves and pursue their dreams. He was a life changer!! Alan had an incredible gift for storytelling, a wonderful sense of humor, an adventurous spirit, and a personality that could fill any room. His life was filled with remarkable experiences, fascinating people, and enough stories for several lifetimes. And he loved sharing them! But behind all those accomplishments was the man I was fortunate enough to call my husband, my partner, and my best friend. We shared a love that was truly special. We loved traveling together, laughing together, and simply being together. We never needed a room full of people or an elaborate plan to enjoy ourselves. We genuinely loved each other’s company. Even after all our years together, life with Alan was never boring. Alan faced more than his share of health challenges over the years, yet he continued to approach life with determination, humor, and gratitude. He fought hard for the life he loved, and I was honored to stand beside him through it all. Several years ago, Alan wrote his autobiography, Lights, Camera, Action and he shared – “It’s been a great ride and I am grateful for every bit of it.” He also wrote that he wanted his children, grandchildren, family, and friends to celebrate his life rather than mourn his passing. That was Alan. He understood that life was an adventure, that tomorrow was never guaranteed, and that the greatest treasures weren’t things, but the people and experiences that made life meaningful. So today, even through my tears, I want to honor his wishes and celebrate the remarkable life he lived. To his sons, Cody and Cooper, all of our incredible family, his friends, his students, and everyone whose life he touched — I hope you’ll remember Alan with a smile, share a favorite story, and celebrate the joy he brought into this world. And to my sweet Alan — thank you for loving me, for making me laugh, for the adventures, the memories, and the beautiful life we built together. I would choose you all over again, without hesitation. My heart is broken, but I am so thankful for the love of a lifetime. I will love you always.

article_text:
10月14日から、和歌山県立近代美術館にて鈴木崇の個展が開催される。写真というメディアを介して、視覚と知覚の関係性や認識の変化に注目し、作品を展開する鈴木崇。鈴木の眼差しを手がかりに不確かなこの世界のあり方を探る。普段の生活のなかで出会う数々のものやイメージ。私たちは視覚を通してさまざまなことを把握している。しかし、それらは実際どのように理解されているのか？「All is not as it seems」（すべてが見かけ通りとは限らない）と、鈴木は問いかける。

本展では、鈴木の新旧作品とともに、作家が選んだ当館コレクションもあわせて展示される。「もののをかし」をテーマに構成した会場によって、視覚と知覚をめぐる思索に誘われてみてはいかが。

タイトル

鈴木崇 もののをかし

場所

和歌山県立近代美術館 2階展示室

会期

2026年10月14日（水）～2027年02月11日（木）

時間

9:30〜17:00（入場は16:30まで）

休館日

月曜日（祝休日の11月23日、2027年1月11日は開館）、11月24日（火）、年末年始（12月28日～ 1月4日）、2027年1月12日（火）

料金

一般600円、大学生330円

https://www.momaw.jp/exhibit/2026suzuki/

Register

Chantal Miller Gallery Asia Society Hong Kong Center 9 Justice Drive Admiralty Tuesday – Sunday, 11am – 6pm +852 2103 9511

asiasociety.org

Inspired by Asia Society Hong Kong Center’s exhibition Singing and Dancing with Brush and Ink: The Art of Wesley Tongson and the Wesley Tongson Archive at Asia Art Archive, Hong Kong artist Wai Pongyu and the ASHK Curatorial Team proudly present UNARCHIVED: Techno & Impermanent Flux.

UNARCHIVED treats performance as an act of raw honesty — a method of reanimating memory not on paper, but through moving bodies. Wai Pongyu approaches the archive as material to be reenacted and rave as an art form, celebrating the dance floor as a source of resilience, freedom, and joy. Expect shifting soundscapes from atmospheric, nostalgic pop to heavy-hitting techno, paired with dynamic visual projections in an environment built on proximity, sweat, and intensity.

Join us for a one-night-only, after-hours activation at Asia Society Hong Kong Center’s Chantal Miller Gallery, translating visual and textual records into a visceral, collective sensory experience.

No re-tracing. No place to hide. Just the flux of the present moment.

This experimental project is made possible through the generous support of our enthusiastic patrons, including Friends and Art Patron Circle of ASHK, Alisan Fine Arts, Brave Art, Christopher Sim, GROTTO, Keiy San, Legacies Collective, Living Ltd., Nomad, Olivia Wang, Wendy Lee, Yardley Brothers Craft Brewery and anonymous supporters. With Media Partner Artomity. We also thank Asia Art Archive for supporting us with archival materials.

article_text:
A monumental sculpture by artist Alicja Kwade will be removed early from public display in Paris, where it was installed part of the public program of the Art Basel Paris fair. The piece is situated on the Avenue Winston Churchill, on the doorstep of the Grand Palais, where the fair is taking place; it went on view today and will be removed on Friday, rather than Sunday, her Paris gallery, Mennour, told ARTnews in an email.

“Unfortunately, only on view today and tomorrow, as it has to be dismantled, along with other sculptures, because of the announced riots and people who simply want to resort to violence,” Kwade told her nearly 100,000 followers in an Instagram post on Wednesday. “Protest is good, but why everything has to be smashed and destroyed is beyond…” she added. “It certainly doesn’t help the cause.”

The New York Times called the Paris protests, which began as a small student movement and blossomed nationwide, “the most destructive riots in decades.” More than half a million marched throughout France on Saturday, according to the Interior Ministry. Many were peaceful but some 1,500 shops and many symbols of the state were vandalized, leading to more than 2,000 arrests. Local authorities imposed curfews.

Kwade’s 2026 piece, L’Élévation des Mondes ( The Elevation of the Worlds ), stands over 14 feet high and is composed of a stack of spheres in materials like rainbow sandstone, black marble, and Carrara marble. According to a description on Mennour’s website, “the sculpture explores questions of world order, power, colonization and humanity’s attempt to construct systems that explain and organize reality. At the same time, it evokes the Tower of Babel—the human desire to reach the stars and the inevitable failure of universal systems of order.” It describes the materials as “witnesses to immense natural catastrophes, tectonic processes, and millions or even billions of years of planetary history.”

Born in Poland in 1979, Kwade lives in Berlin. Besides Mennour, the artist works with New York’s 303 Gallery and Pace Gallery, Reykjavik’s i8 Gallery, and Gallery OMR in Mexico City, according to her website. Her work appears in museum collections from the Centre Pompidou in Paris to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and the Yuz Museum in Shanghai, and she has been included in major international exhibitions including the 2017 Venice Biennale, “Viva Arte Viva,” curated by Christine Macel.

Also on view at the same site as Kwade are works by Simone Fattal, Carmen Herrera, Marcello Maloberti, Keita Miyazaki, Manfred Pernice, Niki de Saint Phalle, and Yinka Shonibare. Press representatives for Art Basel did not immediately respond to ARTnews ’s inquiry about whether other works will also be removed early.

Neben den mainstreamigen Genrestoffen gibt es bei Netflix aber immer wieder auch außergewöhnlicheres Arthousekino aus Südkorea zu entdecken. article_text:
Lee Chang-dongs feinfühliges Drama „Possible Love“ hat nach seinem Festival-Erfolg in Venedig nun seinem Streamingstart. Außerdem starten eine Reihe neuer Weihnachtsfilme, die zweite Staffel der schwarzkomödiantischen Agentenserie „Black Doves“ sowie der „Oscar“-Erfolg „Blood & Sinners“.

Gleich nach den USA ist Südkorea das erfolgreichste und wichtigste Produktionsland von Netflix: Koreanische Filme und Serien gehören zu den weltweiten Hits des Streamingdiensts, von Thrillern à la „ Squid Game “ über Actionfilme wie „ Carter “ bis zu den unzähligen K-Romances wie „ Can This Love Be Translated “. Neben den mainstreamigen Genrestoffen gibt es bei Netflix aber immer wieder auch außergewöhnlicheres Arthousekino aus Südkorea zu entdecken. Das jüngste Beispiel dafür ist das Drama „ Possible Love “, das im September beim Filmfestival in Venedig Premiere feierte, dort hymnisches Lob sowie den „Großen Preis der Jury“ einheimste und nun nach einem Kinostart im Oktober ab 6. November bei Netflix streambar ist.

Der Film ist die jüngste Arbeit des südkoreanischen Altmeisters Lee Chang-dong , der sich mit „Possible Love“ ganze acht Jahre nach „ Burning “ auf fulminante Weise zurückmeldet. In stattlichen 164 Minuten Laufzeit entfaltet der Film die Geschichte einer ungleichen Freundschaft zwischen zwei Familien, einem Ehepaar mit kleinem Sohn aus der Arbeiterschicht sowie einer Filmemacherin und ihrem Millionärs-Ehemann. Der Kontakt kommt zustande, weil die Filmemacherin im Rahmen eines Dokumentarfilmprojekts Interviews mit der Working-Class-Familie führen will. Diese steckt in einer Krise, seit der Job des Mannes in einer Fabrik wegrationalisiert wurde, und vor allem der Frau scheint es gutzutun, endlich auf jemanden zu treffen, der ein offenes Ohr hat für das, was ihr Mann und der Rest der Familie dadurch durchmachen. Aus den Dreharbeiten entsteht eine Annäherung zwischen den Paaren – und doch bleiben soziale Gräben zwischen ihnen. Statt eines bitterbösen Clashs zwischen Arm und Reich zeigt „Possible Love“ ein schillerndes Beziehungsviereck, in dem keine der Figuren auf ihre Funktion als Klassen-Stellvertreter reduziert wird; das Persönliche und Zwischenmenschliche lässt sich aber auch nie ganz von den sozialen Rollen, Prägungen und Kräfteverhältnissen lösen.

Aktuelle Streaming-Kritiken

(Vor)Weihnachtliches

Außerdem startet bei Netflix im November noch ein weiterer Film, der dieses Jahr in Venedig Premiere hatte: Im französischen Drama „ Ein guter Anwalt “, das beim Festival außer Konkurrenz lief, spielt Laurent Lafitte einen Strafverteidiger mit Drogenproblemen, der nach einem Überdosis-bedingten Zusammenbruch vor Gericht und einem Entzug sein Leben wieder in den Griff kriegen und seine Karriere retten muss. Ansonsten merkt man dem Netflix-Filmprogramm im November an, dass es, sobald die Tage länger werden, langsam auf den Advent zugeht: Zu den Neustarts des Streamingdienstes gehören diverse neue Weihnachtsfilme. Das Spektrum reicht vom neuen Tyler-Perry-Drama „ The Gospel of Christmas “ (ab 11. November), in dem ein von Schicksalsschlägen und Glaubenszweifeln geplagter Pastor, angespornt von seiner charakter- und glaubensstarken Frau, darum zu kämpfen beginnt, seine Gemeinde und seine Kirche in einem schwierigen Viertel von New York vor dem Aus zu bewahren, bis zur schwedischen Liebeskomödie „ Nur bis Weihnachten “ (ab 12. November).

Außerdem gibt es auch vorweihnachtliche Familien-Unterhaltung mit einem tierischen Helden: In „ Winstead – Ein Hund feiert Weihnachten “ (zu sehen ab 4.11.) geht es um einen schlappohrigen Basset, der dafür sorgen muss, dass sein grantiges, verwitwetes Senioren-Herrchen (Dennis Quaid) sich zum Fest etwas öffnet und vor allem wieder mit seiner Enkelin zusammenrauft.

Spionagestoffe und eine unheimliche Schule

Wer es lieber spannend statt herzig mag, wird bei Netflix im November unter anderem bei einer zweiten Staffel der britischen Agentenserie „ Black Doves “ mit Keira Knightley fündig. Ihre Figur, die als Spionin einer klandestinen Organisation undercover als Frau eines Politikers Regierungsgeheimnisse ausspäht, war im Lauf der ersten Staffel auf brandgefährliche Weise in Bedrängnis geraten und hatte Unterstützung von einem alten Freund und Kollegen (Ben Whishaw) bekommen; in Staffel 2 müssen sich die beiden nun weiter durch einen Wust an Intrigen und Geheimnissen kämpfen. Dabei kommen diverse neue Figuren ins Spiel, unter anderem verkörpert von Ambika Mod, Sam Riley und Neve Campbell.

Außerdem gibt es einen Serienneustart, der mit dem Unheimlichen und religiöser Hysterie flirtet: In der US-Produktion „ The Body “, zu sehen ab 11. November, geht es um beunruhigende Entwicklungen an einer katholischen Mädchenschule: Showrunnerin Quinn Shephard stellt eine Schul-Tanzgruppe ins Zentrum, deren Mitglieder, nachdem die Initiation eines neuen Mitglieds im Rahmen einer Party wüst eskaliert ist, plötzlich angeblich prophetische Visionen haben, was über die Schule hinaus zu Aufruhr und Massenhysterie führt.

Nervenaufreibend geht es auch in einem neuen Film von Shana Feste zu, „ Heartland “: Jessica Chastain verkörpert einen einstigen Country-Star, der sich desillusioniert längst von den Bühnen in Nashville zurückgezogen hat, dann aber zurückkehrt: Die Nichte der Musikerin, selbst ein aufstrebender Star in der Country-Hochburg, ist verschwunden, und die Tante macht sich auf die Suche. Dabei muss sie sich ihrer eigenen Vergangenheit stellen und stößt auf die dunklen Geheimnisse Nashvilles.

Doku über einen prägenden Fotografen

Außerdem hat Netflix auch wieder Dokumentarisches im Programm: Ab 11. November beleuchtet das Doku-Porträt „ Avedon “ Leben und Schaffen des berühmten Fotografen Richard Avedon, der in den 1940er-Jahren zu einem der prägendsten Modefotografen des 20. Jahrhunderts aufstieg. Der Film arbeitet, so die Netflix-Ankündigung, dank Zugriff auf Avedons persönliches Archiv mit bisher unveröffentlichten Bildern; außerdem baut er auf Interviews mit Avedons engsten Mitarbeiter:innen, um zu beleuchten, „wie seine einzigartige Perspektive die Bildsprache des 20. Jahrhunderts sowohl wiedergab als auch formte“.

Freuen können sich Netflix-Kund:innen außerdem auf einen hochkarätigen Katalogtitel: Ab 3. November zeigt Netflix den ungewöhnlichen Horrorfilm „ Blood & Sinners “, der einer der großen Gewinner bei den „Oscars“ 2026 war. Der Film von Ryan Coogler mischt reale Schrecken mit Fantastischem: Ein afroamerikanisches Zwillingsbrüder-Paar lässt in den 1930er-Jahren das Gangsterdasein in Chicago hinter sich, um in seiner Heimat in Mississippi neu anzufangen, und zwar mit einer Tanzbar für die schwarze Community. Doch dabei kommt ihnen nicht nur der Ku-Klux-Klan in die Quere, sondern auch eine Gruppe von Vampiren.

article_text:
Fleetwood Mac : The Chain , the first fully authorized documentary on the legendary rock band, will debut on Apple TV on January 29, 2027.

The documentary, directed by Frank Marshall and produced by The Kennedy/Marshall Company and White Horse Pictures, offers fans what Apple has described as a “definitive and unprecedented look at Fleetwood Mac’s story, bringing together voices, memories and perspectives of Grammy Award-winning Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductees Mick Fleetwood, John McVie, Christine McVie, Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks.”

The doc synopsis reads: Following their fortuitous meeting in 1974, Mick Fleetwood, John McVie, Christine McVie, Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks reflect on their uncompromising 50-plus-year history, from their record-breaking recordings and tours — including never-before-seen footage and exclusive new interviews — through to today.

The film will explore how the band’s trials and tribulations, personal resilience, and musical dexterity combined to create enduring masterpieces. It will take fans through the highs and lows of their brilliant career, illuminating the exceptional ingredients each member brought to the band’s uncommon alchemy — a musical union that sold more than 220 million records worldwide.

title_original: ‘Fighting an impossible fight is the only way to reclaim dignity’: Lee Chang-dong on class warfare and his searing Oscar contender

"translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在时事通讯推广之后", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在李沧东的讲述中，他成为导演几乎纯属偶然。20世纪80年代，身为韩国作家的他身处军事独裁政府统治之下，感到自己有责任唤起人们对人类苦难的关注：“那是我们的道义责任。”随着韩国走向民主并迈入新世纪，他感到尽管苦难依然存在，“文学界人们心中的这种道义责任却开始消失。探讨现实切肤之痛的文学被当作过期商品对待。我对这种转变感到失望。”他转而尝试编剧以求新意，随后又担任副导演，“因为我某种程度上几乎是想惩罚自己，让自己经历非常艰难的事情。我工作得如此努力，以至于周围的人都被打动了，他们说：‘哦，你应该去当导演。’\"", "如今的韩国电影以直面资本主义的残酷描绘而闻名于世，不过，与奉俊昊的《寄生虫》（其中也刻画了两个家庭之间的阶级鸿沟）或朴赞郁的《无可奈何》（同样讲述企业裁员的悲惨）不同，李沧东的角色并不是那种对体制发起反抗、最终却只获得痛苦而堕落胜利的心机之徒。相反，我们往往只能在一旁观察他们是如何被周围的世界边缘化；我们见证他们微小的失望、他们所忍受的残忍，以及他们如何咬紧牙关去守住希望。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，他的电影也展现了这些角色所找到的那些虽小却意义重大的慰藉与优雅：在自然中、在其他人身上，或是依靠他们自己的意志力。李沧东此前曾将自己的电影形容为关于人们对抗庞大、不可逾越的庞然大物、进行不可能获胜的斗争的故事。“然而，尽管如此，我认为斗争本身是有意义的。我认为这些个人与世界的抗争，很可能是他们重新宣示尊严的唯一途径。无论你获胜的机会有多大，我认为斗争本身就是意义重大且富有价值的。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在威尼斯电影节斩获大奖后，关于奥斯卡奖的讨论已经悄然传开；该片已成为韩国角逐最佳国际影片的代表作品。我问他成功对意味着什么。“我拍电影总是希望能与观众建立连接。每当观众能够接受我在电影中提出的问题并试图找到他们自己的答案时，对我来说都意义重大。希望这能给他们的生活带来哪怕极其微小的改变。”对于一位长期以来刻画人们如何对充满敌意的世界开展微小抵抗、并在细微变化中看到希望的导演而言，这是一个再贴切不过的回答。", They’re on their way to a funeral of Ho-seok’s former colleague, who killed himself after being made redundant, and meet the ambitious film-maker Lee Ye-ji and her financier husband Sang-woo. They radiate the kind of glow afforded by wealth. After a stay at a luxury resort in Qatar made Ye-ji reflect on the nature of hidden labour, she’s making a film about the state of labour in Korea, and believes she’s found her ideal subjects; if only Ho-seok, who refuses to go to therapy let alone talk about his experiences in front of a camera, would agree."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Since his first feature in 1997, Lee, now 72, has made luminous yet unsparing films about disempowered people swept up in brutal economic and political circumstances: his protagonists include blue-collar workers, ex-prisoners, people with disabilities. In his previous film Burning, an adaptation of a Haruki Murakami short story, a poor writer battles for a woman’s affections with a wealthier rival. (Possible Love brings together two lead actors from Lee’s most acclaimed films; Secret Sunshine’s Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu who starred Peppermint Candy and Oasis.) Class tensions bristle throughout his work: now, however, he’s wondering whether we’ve outstripped the usefulness of the term."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“It’s difficult to use the word ‘class’ because it is so vast,” he says of the difference between the couples in Possible Love. It’s about how he is capable of moving and controlling a huge amount of capital. And that capital creates further wealth. It’s almost as if you can’t really grasp how much wealth it creates. It’s just something of a different dimension.” At the same time, “I didn’t want to show that the two couples belong to completely different worlds, because they do live in the same world.” It is, after all, the abstract financial machinations of people like Sang-woo that materially overturn the lives of people like Ho-seok. Ye-ji has a habit of holding her camera up at inappropriate moments, often to the discomfort of Mi-ok and Ho-seok’s young son, Cheol. I wonder if she’s supposed to be a sympathetic character. “Anyone who’s really hardworking, they tend to overdo it,” Lee says. He feels a “closeness” to her, “and cameras by their nature search for drama.” Can there ever be equality between a film-maker and their subject? “It’s very hard to be equal because the person holding the camera without even realising it is given power. Literature that dealt with the close pains of reality were treated as if they were expired goods. I was disappointed with that change.” He took up screenwriting to try something new, before working as an assistant director, “because I almost wanted to punish myself in a way, make myself go through something very tough. I worked so hard at it that people around me were moved, and they said: ‘Oh, you should be a film-maker.’”", "links": [{"text": "South Korea", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/world/south-korea"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "South Korean films today are known globally for their confronting depictions of capitalism, though unlike, say, Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite (which also features a class divide between two families) or Park Chan-wook’s No Other Choice (also about the misery of corporate layoffs), Lee’s characters are not schemers who attain pyrrhic, depraved victory against the system. We instead are often left to observe how they are marginalised by the world around them; we witness their small disappointments, the cruelties they endure, and how they strain to hold on to their hopes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yet his films also reveal the small but significant moments of solace and grace these characters find: in nature, other people, or their own willpower. Lee has previously described his films as stories about people taking on impossible fights against large, impenetrable entities. “However, despite that, I think the fight itself has meaning. I think these fights the individuals take on against the world is quite possibly the only way they are able to reclaim dignity. Regardless of your chances of winning, I think the fight itself is significant and meaningful.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You could say that his latest film was made after a fight of sorts. Netflix stepped in to fund it, granting the film a theatrical release in some countries worldwide. “The character Ye-ji has a wealthy husband. She lives with someone who holds that capital but still tries her best to be independent,” Lee says. (Her husband, Sang-woo, somewhat disparagingly describes an independent film as a “film independent of capital”; “I thought it would be very amusing to have him say that line,” says Lee.) “I feel like she and I are in the same shoes. And hopefully that leads to a very small change in their lives.” It’s a fitting answer for a film-maker who has long portrayed the subtle acts of resistance people can mount against a hostile world; who finds in small changes, causes for hope."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Possible Love is in cinemas now, and on Netflix November 6."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Film", "links": [{"text": "Film", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/film"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Venice film festival", "links": [{"text": "Venice film festival", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/venicefilmfestival"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "South Korea", "links": [{"text": "South Korea", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/world/south-korea"}]}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "interviews", "links": [{"text": "interviews", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/tone/interview"}]}]
article_text:
A quintessential 21st-century horror story: a private equity firm has set its sights on your company. That’s the premise behind director Lee Chang-dong’s new film, Possible Love, and the idea for it first came more than a decade ago, when mass layoffs resulted in a standoff that “fundamentally changed the Korean labour movement”.

In 2009, workers at Ssangyong Motors company protested against plans to lay off between 37 and 43% of the workforce, staging a historic 77-day strike and occupation of the factory that was eventually broken up by riot police. “Until that point in time in Korea, labourers’ rights were widely accepted,” Lee says, speaking through an interpreter in a central London hotel; “however, afterwards, the basic rights of labourers changed; to the public, they couldn’t be seen as more important than market profitability or corporate competitiveness.”

At the time, Lee shelved the project. “The more I examined the pain of these individuals” – after the violent crackdown on the Ssangyong Motors strike, there were several suicides, and reports of long-term mental health issues – “I constantly asked myself: am I worthy of telling this story? And if I am, how do I tell it? Do I stand close to the workers, or keep my distance?” Later he and his co-writer Oh Jung-mi, wrote “many different” scripts, including one with post-apocalyptic elements, before Oh suggested introducing a character who is a documentary film-maker, thereby finding a way to work in Lee’s ambivalence about his intentions.

The result is a sharply observed Russian doll of a film that places a narrative about “labour and its relationship to capital” within a broader story about the ethics of film-making, and the tensions and desires that emerge when a working-class couple collide with an astronomically wealthy one. It has, like many of Lee’s previous films, been received to great acclaim: it recently won the grand jury prize at Venice film festival , and has been hailed by critics as one of the best films of the year.

The film’s opening title shows the 10th commandment, “Thou shalt not covet”. You can already guess that it will be swiftly broken. Soon we see the depressed Ho-seok, who has been fired from his job at a metal factory, reprimanding his free-spirited wife Mi-ok for caring about her clothes. They’re on their way to a funeral of Ho-seok’s former colleague, who killed himself after being made redundant, and meet the ambitious film-maker Lee Ye-ji and her financier husband Sang-woo. They radiate the kind of glow afforded by wealth. After a stay at a luxury resort in Qatar made Ye-ji reflect on the nature of hidden labour, she’s making a film about the state of labour in Korea, and believes she’s found her ideal subjects; if only Ho-seok, who refuses to go to therapy let alone talk about his experiences in front of a camera, would agree.

Since his first feature in 1997, Lee, now 72, has made luminous yet unsparing films about disempowered people swept up in brutal economic and political circumstances: his protagonists include blue-collar workers, ex-prisoners, people with disabilities. In his previous film Burning, an adaptation of a Haruki Murakami short story, a poor writer battles for a woman’s affections with a wealthier rival. (Possible Love brings together two lead actors from Lee’s most acclaimed films; Secret Sunshine’s Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu who starred Peppermint Candy and Oasis.) Class tensions bristle throughout his work: now, however, he’s wondering whether we’ve outstripped the usefulness of the term.

“It’s difficult to use the word ‘class’ because it is so vast,” he says of the difference between the couples in Possible Love. He describes Sang-woo, who moves about the world with possessive ease, an allure and emptiness, as a “symbol of capital … It’s not even that Sang-woo is a wealthy man. It’s about how he is capable of moving and controlling a huge amount of capital. And that capital creates further wealth. It’s almost as if you can’t really grasp how much wealth it creates. It’s just something of a different dimension.” At the same time, “I didn’t want to show that the two couples belong to completely different worlds, because they do live in the same world.” It is, after all, the abstract financial machinations of people like Sang-woo that materially overturn the lives of people like Ho-seok. Making the characters interact together at restaurants, their homes, and on a charged summer holiday “was going to naturally bring out the tension, the hidden power difference between them. There is a gap that just cannot be crossed.”

The film exposes the audience to many different kinds of looking: we are shown Ye-ji’s documentary footage; a CCTV feed; newsreel-style clips of a violent police crackdown on a workers’ strike. Lee wanted to study the “issue of the gaze”; “the ethics of capturing and observing the lives and pain of others”. Ye-ji has a habit of holding her camera up at inappropriate moments, often to the discomfort of Mi-ok and Ho-seok’s young son, Cheol. I wonder if she’s supposed to be a sympathetic character. “Anyone who’s really hardworking, they tend to overdo it,” Lee says. He feels a “closeness” to her, “and cameras by their nature search for drama.” Can there ever be equality between a film-maker and their subject? “It’s very hard to be equal because the person holding the camera without even realising it is given power. And it’s a one-sided relationship.”

after newsletter promotion

In his telling, Lee became a film-maker almost by accident. He was a writer in 1980s South Korea , then under a military government, feeling called to draw attention to human suffering: “That was our moral responsibility.” As the country moved towards democracy and into the new century, he felt that although the suffering still remained, “that moral responsibility among people in literature began to disappear. Literature that dealt with the close pains of reality were treated as if they were expired goods. I was disappointed with that change.” He took up screenwriting to try something new, before working as an assistant director, “because I almost wanted to punish myself in a way, make myself go through something very tough. I worked so hard at it that people around me were moved, and they said: ‘Oh, you should be a film-maker.’”

South Korean films today are known globally for their confronting depictions of capitalism, though unlike, say, Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite (which also features a class divide between two families) or Park Chan-wook’s No Other Choice (also about the misery of corporate layoffs), Lee’s characters are not schemers who attain pyrrhic, depraved victory against the system. We instead are often left to observe how they are marginalised by the world around them; we witness their small disappointments, the cruelties they endure, and how they strain to hold on to their hopes.

Yet his films also reveal the small but significant moments of solace and grace these characters find: in nature, other people, or their own willpower. Lee has previously described his films as stories about people taking on impossible fights against large, impenetrable entities. “However, despite that, I think the fight itself has meaning. I think these fights the individuals take on against the world is quite possibly the only way they are able to reclaim dignity. Regardless of your chances of winning, I think the fight itself is significant and meaningful.”

You could say that his latest film was made after a fight of sorts. Lee struggled to find domestic funding for the film, given the “structural crisis” facing the Korean industry, caused by the economic losses from a strict Covid 19 lockdown, and the rise of streaming services. Netflix stepped in to fund it, granting the film a theatrical release in some countries worldwide. “The character Ye-ji has a wealthy husband. She lives with someone who holds that capital but still tries her best to be independent,” Lee says. (Her husband, Sang-woo, somewhat disparagingly describes an independent film as a “film independent of capital”; “I thought it would be very amusing to have him say that line,” says Lee.) “I feel like she and I are in the same shoes. I am also dependent on capital to get my films made. You could say that I am also someone who is married to capital, but trying to protect my own voice, which I almost think is the fate of all film-makers.”

After its victory at Venice, there are already whispers about the Oscars; it is South Korea’s submission for best international feature. I ask what success means to him. “I’ve always made films wanting to connect with audiences. It’s always meaningful for me when my audiences accept the questions that I ask through my films and try to find their own answers. And hopefully that leads to a very small change in their lives.” It’s a fitting answer for a film-maker who has long portrayed the subtle acts of resistance people can mount against a hostile world; who finds in small changes, causes for hope.

Possible Love is in cinemas now, and on Netflix November 6.

"安德烈·刘易斯：对我而言，matereality是材料与生活现实变得密不可分的那个节点。材料绝非中立：它们自带历史、联想、劳作、政治、记忆以及早已附着其上的社会现实。一条毛毯在成为艺术品之前就有着自身的含义。头发有含义。泥土有含义。水泥袋、衣物、塑料、珠子、肥皂或电子垃圾都承载着社会和文化联想。艺术家们激活了这些历史。这些材料并非仅仅是颜料、青铜或大理石的不寻常替代品；它们的意义与作品本身的意义是密不可分的。材料并非围绕构思的装饰。它本身就是构思的一部分。", "最初的“Matereality”源于我在ISANG（伊兹科南非国家美术馆）注意到的一种现象：艺术家们越来越多地超越传统媒介，其方式挑战了博物馆所依赖的各种分类。绘画融入了橡胶、头发、机油、纺织品和现成品。雕塑则汲取自手工艺、工业、服装和行为表演。绘画、雕塑、纺织品、装置以及纸本作品之间的界限越来越难以维持。那个展览囊括了当时已经非常知名的艺术家，包括伊格沙恩·亚当斯（Igshaan Adams）和乌莎·西贾里姆（Usha Seejarim），以及许多其他刻意用非常规材料进行实验的艺术家。然后COVID爆发了。展览于2020年开幕，几乎立刻就进入了博物馆和画廊纷纷关闭的奇异时期。但这个想法留在了我的脑海中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "六年之后，背景再次发生了转变。我们正经历着非凡的数字加速和人工智能的迅猛崛起，而许多艺术家却将大量时间投入到高度物质化的过程中：缝纫、编织、切割、装订、分层、组装和重复。我不认为这是对技术的排斥，但在一个日益去物质化的世界里，实体创作感觉更加重要。材料具有分量、质感、阻力和物质存在感。“Matereality "它们是有机地融入的，因为材料与地方有着深厚的联系。艺术家们利用身边的文化、经济、环境和政治事物进行创作。在南非，材料可以承载极其复杂的历史。它们可以讲述采矿与开采、土地与流离失所、外来劳工、服装与身份、家政劳动、不平等、环境退化、灵性、本土知识体系以及创作历史。但我并不希望这些主题变成整齐划一的类别。我不希望一个展厅全纺织品，另一个展厅全塑料，别的地方又全是现成物。有趣的部分恰恰在于这些历史与材料是如何交织在一起的。与此同时，我不希望展览暗示南非艺术家似乎仅仅在回应南非的关切。这些实践与围绕气候变化、消费、移民、技术、可持续性和归属感的更大问题息息相关。这也是展览将范围延伸至南非以外、聚焦该大陆其他地区精选艺术家的原因之一。整个非洲正在发生非凡的材料实验，通常使用的是那些具有地方特异性、同时又能对话全球系统与关切的物品或物质。吸引我的正是这种在本土与普遍之间的流动。一种材料可能在开普敦、约翰内斯堡、阿克拉或哈拉雷有着高度特定的社会历史，但该艺术品可以同时开启关于当代生活的更广泛对话。“Matereality "我希望人们离开展览时，能以不同的眼光看待寻常材料。我们生活在各种物品和物质之中，而它们的历史我们却很少去思考：它们来自何方、是谁制作的、其中包含了多少劳动力、是怎样的贸易或开采系统生产了它们、它们承载着怎样的环境代价，以及它们最终将去往何处。艺术家特别擅长打破这种熟悉感。他们能把我们以为自己很了解的东西变得陌生。价值问题在这里至关重要。为什么某种材料被认为是珍贵的，而另一种则被视为一次性的？为什么某些创作形式被称为艺术，而历史上另一些则被归类为手工艺、家务劳动或装饰？谁来决定什么值得保护？我还希望人们在离开时会去思考作品之间的关系。我花了多年时间在脑海中甚至字面上揣摩这些图像，逐渐看到了那些可能从未想过会并肩展示的艺术家之间的联系。但一旦展览开幕，这些关系就不再只属于我。参观者可能会在两件作品之间看到完全不同的联系——通过某种材料、一段记忆、一种颜色、一段历史或一种经历。我喜欢这种想法：展览可以持续引发超越我刻意构建的对话。因此，它或许会给参观者留下一些相当简单的问题：我们日常遇到的物品中包含着哪些历史？它们的背后凝聚了谁的劳动力？为什么我们珍视某些东西而抛弃另一些？当同一种材料能够同时象征舒适与暴力、熟悉与剥削、亲密感与庞大的全球体系时，会发生什么？一旦我们不再仅仅从预定功能去看待一种材料，它又可能存在哪些潜能？当然，以物质性为中心的展览极为常见，艺术家们几个世纪以来也一直在研究材料。我当然不是在暗示《Matereality V2》引入了全新的东西。我更希望将当代创作中贯穿的众多线索——劳动力、生态、本土知识、手工艺、记忆、技术、消费和价值——汇聚起来，看看当它们被综合考量时，会呈现出什么。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从这个意义上说，《Matereality V2》或许是一个盘点的契机：它是对我在过去几年里所观察到的一切的一种总结，也是对新兴和成熟艺术家如何以非凡的创造力将材料与意义融为一体的一种概括。我希望它能为那场更为漫长的对话贡献新的篇章。或许，它也能鼓励我们更加密切地关注周围的事物——关注材料本身所蕴含的内容、其中嵌入的劳动力与历史，以及当艺术家拿走一件熟悉的事物并让我们以完全不同的方式看待它时会发生什么。", "translated": In ‘Materiality V2’, curator Andrea Lewis brings together emerging and established artists whose practices challenge conventional distinctions between art, craft and everyday life. From textiles and found objects to industrial waste and organic matter, the exhibition reveals how materials carry histories of extraction, cultural knowledge, human experience and transformation."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In conversation with ART AFRICA, Lewis reflects on the evolving relationship between material and meaning, the importance of physical making in an increasingly digital world, and museums’ role in reconsidering what we preserve, value, and remember. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Suzette Bell-Roberts: The title ‘Matereality V2’ brings together material and reality. In this exhibition, what does “matereality” mean, and how has that idea evolved in this second iteration?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Andrea Lewis: For me, matereality is the point at which material and lived reality become inseparable. Materials are never neutral: they arrive with histories, associations, labour, politics, memory and social realities already attached to them. A blanket means something before it becomes an artwork. Hair means something. Soil means something. A cement bag, clothing, plastic, beads, soap or electronic waste all carry social and cultural associations. Artists activate those histories. These materials are not simply unusual substitutes for paint, bronze or marble; their meanings are inseparable from the meanings of the works themselves. The material is not decoration around the idea. It is part of the idea."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The first ‘Matereality’ developed out of something I had been noticing at ISANG: artists were increasingly moving beyond traditional media in ways that challenged the categories museums rely upon. Paintings incorporated rubber, hair, engine oil, textiles and found objects. Sculpture drew from craft, industry, clothing and performance. The distinctions between painting, sculpture, textiles, installation and works on paper were becoming increasingly difficult to maintain. That exhibition included artists who were already very well known, including Igshaan Adams and Usha Seejarim, alongside many others experimenting deliberately with unconventional materials. And then COVID happened. The exhibition opened in 2020 and almost immediately entered this strange period in which museums and galleries were closing. But the idea stayed with me."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Six years later, the context has shifted again. We are living through extraordinary digital acceleration and the rapid rise of artificial intelligence, while many artists are investing enormous amounts of time in intensely physical processes: stitching, weaving, cutting, binding, layering, assembling and repeating. I do not necessarily see this as a rejection of technology, but physical making feels more significant in an increasingly dematerialised world. Materials have weight, texture, resistance and physical presence. So ‘Matereality V2’ gives us insight into the realities of individual artists, but also into the state of the world around us. Through material, it opens onto questions of land and belonging, labour and the body, memory and family, indigenous knowledge, colonial histories, consumption and waste, environmental concerns, and value. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "How were the artists and works for ‘Matereality V2’ selected , and what conversations emerged among their different practices?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The selection process began while the first ‘Matereality’ was still on exhibition. I started writing down the names of artists I wished I had known about, or had been able to include, the first time around – artists such as Sepideh Mehraban, Gaelen Pinnock and Promise Mapondera. That list stayed pinned to my wall for the next six years. Whenever I encountered a work that made me think differently about material, I would add the artist’s name. Sometimes that happened in an exhibition, during a studio visit, at an art fair, in the news, or even on Instagram. I would then do a deeper dive into the artist’s practice and, wherever possible, visit their studio and speak to them. Sometimes an artist also made something specifically with this exhibition in mind."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eventually the list grew to around 150 artists, so the difficulty was not finding enough work. It was deciding what to leave out. There are many artists I would dearly have loved to include. For that reason, I do not see ‘Matereality V2’ as a definitive survey. It is more a bird’s-eye view of what I have been noticing over the past few years – a snapshot of emerging and established artists finding inventive ways to make material inseparable from meaning. The process also became very visual. I had images of the works with me and, over time, I found myself linking particular works together. Sometimes those connections were material, but often they were conceptual, emotional or contradictory."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For example, I began thinking about Warren Maroon’s work in relation to Senzeni Marasela’s because both opened up complicated ideas around home – home as a place of comfort, intimacy and belonging, but also of pain, absence or difficulty. I also realised that placing Sepideh Mehraban’s work alongside Ben Stanwix and Xhanti Zwelendaba’s BAWA work created an interesting conversation around place and printing. In different ways, both use imprinting and reproduction to think about how place is recorded, remembered and mediated. From there, Mehraban’s work connected very strongly to Tamlin Blake’s. Mehraban’s carpet carries newspaper imprints, while Blake works directly with newspaper and references book burning. Both bring to mind the ways authoritarian societies can limit access to knowledge and, in doing so, restrict individual autonomy. The newspaper becomes more than a material or source image; it carries questions of information, censorship, power and who is allowed access to knowledge. Gaelen Pinnock’s work began speaking to Lungisa Qwanta’s in ways that became clearer the longer I lived with the images."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Other pairings came almost instinctively. I could not resist placing Yonela Makoba’s teabag work in conversation with Zaneaca Singh’s sugar works. Tea and sugar are so intimately linked to comfort, hospitality and everyday ritual, yet both are deeply entangled with colonial trade, extraction and systems whose consequences continue to be felt today. Atang Tshikare and Lyndi Sales were another pairing that became exciting to me. Their works open onto connections between cosmology, science, plants, natural systems and forms of knowledge that move between the earthly and the speculative. I placed the work of Chris Soal in conversation with Hanien Conradie’s work. Soal found the bottle caps he uses in the streets of Johannesburg, while Conradie gathered her materials from riverbanks and plants. I was interested in that contrast between the inorganic and the organic – two artists collecting from their immediate environments but encountering very different traces of place. One gathers the discarded remnants of an urban and consumer landscape; the other works with materials embedded in natural systems. I also put Sahlah Davids and Jeanne Gaigher in the same room. Both had been working abstractly and, for works made specifically for this exhibition, began experimenting with figuration. I loved that parallel: two artists independently shifting their visual languages and then finding themselves in conversation within the exhibition."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There are many more connections, and they became central to the curatorial process. One work would lead me to another, sometimes through material, sometimes through process, and sometimes through a shared political or emotional concern. The exhibition gradually became a web of relationships rather than a series of isolated objects. At one stage I considered making the exhibition entirely South African. There was certainly enough work to do that. But ultimately, it felt too restrictive, partly because of the political moment we are living through, when xenophobia and increasingly narrow ideas about nationality and belonging remain so present, but also because this kind of material experimentation is something I have noticed strongly across the African continent."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The final selection was never simply about finding unusual materials. I was interested in artists for whom material is fundamental to the meaning of the work – where you could not simply substitute one material for another without changing what the artwork is saying. That is also why I am drawn to thematic exhibitions. They allow artists across race, gender, age, generation, geography, medium and levels of recognition to enter into a shared conversation. Their differences are not erased, but neither are they confined to fixed categories. Instead, the question becomes: what might very different artists contribute to the same conversation? I am always interested in creating encounters between works that might otherwise never occupy the same room. At the same time, I do not want to explain every connection. Some relationships are quite deliberate, and others emerged unexpectedly, and I hope audiences discover many of them for themselves. A viewer may make a connection that I did not anticipate at all, and that is part of what makes an exhibition alive. Image Courtesy of Gallery.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Material can carry histories of place, labour, culture and exchange. How does the exhibition explore meaning gathered through use, movement and transformation?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Many of the materials in ‘Matereality V2’ have already had lives before they enter the museum. They have circulated through homes, industries, communities, ceremonies, economies or systems of trade and consumption. Through cutting, stitching, weaving, assembling, burning, layering, binding or repetition, those meanings can shift again. Something disposable can become precious. An ordinary domestic material can become political. An industrial product can suddenly speak about the body, land, memory or belonging. As the exhibition developed, I found myself returning to Jane Bennett’s idea of “vibrant matter”. Bennett asks us to reconsider the assumption that matter is passive – that human beings act upon materials and materials obediently receive that action. Instead, she encourages us to think of materials as having their own properties, behaviours and capacities. That became very useful to me while thinking through ‘Matereality’, because artists do not always completely control their materials. Materials sag, crack, stretch, absorb, rust, decay, reflect and resist. Sometimes the artist is working with the material rather than simply imposing something upon it. article_text:
At the Iziko South African National Gallery, ‘Matereality V2’ explores how contemporary artists across Africa transform everyday materials into powerful expressions of memory, identity, labour and belonging.

What happens when the materials we overlook become the very substance of artistic meaning? In ‘Materiality V2’, curator Andrea Lewis brings together emerging and established artists whose practices challenge conventional distinctions between art, craft and everyday life. From textiles and found objects to industrial waste and organic matter, the exhibition reveals how materials carry histories of extraction, cultural knowledge, human experience and transformation.

In conversation with ART AFRICA, Lewis reflects on the evolving relationship between material and meaning, the importance of physical making in an increasingly digital world, and museums’ role in reconsidering what we preserve, value, and remember. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

Suzette Bell-Roberts: The title ‘Matereality V2’ brings together material and reality. In this exhibition, what does “matereality” mean, and how has that idea evolved in this second iteration?

Andrea Lewis: For me, matereality is the point at which material and lived reality become inseparable. Materials are never neutral: they arrive with histories, associations, labour, politics, memory and social realities already attached to them. A blanket means something before it becomes an artwork. Hair means something. Soil means something. A cement bag, clothing, plastic, beads, soap or electronic waste all carry social and cultural associations. Artists activate those histories. These materials are not simply unusual substitutes for paint, bronze or marble; their meanings are inseparable from the meanings of the works themselves. The material is not decoration around the idea. It is part of the idea.

The first ‘Matereality’ developed out of something I had been noticing at ISANG: artists were increasingly moving beyond traditional media in ways that challenged the categories museums rely upon. Paintings incorporated rubber, hair, engine oil, textiles and found objects. Sculpture drew from craft, industry, clothing and performance. The distinctions between painting, sculpture, textiles, installation and works on paper were becoming increasingly difficult to maintain. That exhibition included artists who were already very well known, including Igshaan Adams and Usha Seejarim, alongside many others experimenting deliberately with unconventional materials. And then COVID happened. The exhibition opened in 2020 and almost immediately entered this strange period in which museums and galleries were closing. But the idea stayed with me.

Six years later, the context has shifted again. We are living through extraordinary digital acceleration and the rapid rise of artificial intelligence, while many artists are investing enormous amounts of time in intensely physical processes: stitching, weaving, cutting, binding, layering, assembling and repeating. I do not necessarily see this as a rejection of technology, but physical making feels more significant in an increasingly dematerialised world. Materials have weight, texture, resistance and physical presence. So ‘Matereality V2’ gives us insight into the realities of individual artists, but also into the state of the world around us. Through material, it opens onto questions of land and belonging, labour and the body, memory and family, indigenous knowledge, colonial histories, consumption and waste, environmental concerns, and value. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

How were the artists and works for ‘Matereality V2’ selected , and what conversations emerged among their different practices?

The selection process began while the first ‘Matereality’ was still on exhibition. I started writing down the names of artists I wished I had known about, or had been able to include, the first time around – artists such as Sepideh Mehraban, Gaelen Pinnock and Promise Mapondera. That list stayed pinned to my wall for the next six years. Whenever I encountered a work that made me think differently about material, I would add the artist’s name. Sometimes that happened in an exhibition, during a studio visit, at an art fair, in the news, or even on Instagram. I would then do a deeper dive into the artist’s practice and, wherever possible, visit their studio and speak to them. Sometimes an artist also made something specifically with this exhibition in mind.

Eventually the list grew to around 150 artists, so the difficulty was not finding enough work. It was deciding what to leave out. There are many artists I would dearly have loved to include. For that reason, I do not see ‘Matereality V2’ as a definitive survey. It is more a bird’s-eye view of what I have been noticing over the past few years – a snapshot of emerging and established artists finding inventive ways to make material inseparable from meaning. The process also became very visual. I had images of the works with me and, over time, I found myself linking particular works together. Sometimes those connections were material, but often they were conceptual, emotional or contradictory.

For example, I began thinking about Warren Maroon’s work in relation to Senzeni Marasela’s because both opened up complicated ideas around home – home as a place of comfort, intimacy and belonging, but also of pain, absence or difficulty. I also realised that placing Sepideh Mehraban’s work alongside Ben Stanwix and Xhanti Zwelendaba’s BAWA work created an interesting conversation around place and printing. In different ways, both use imprinting and reproduction to think about how place is recorded, remembered and mediated. From there, Mehraban’s work connected very strongly to Tamlin Blake’s. Mehraban’s carpet carries newspaper imprints, while Blake works directly with newspaper and references book burning. Both bring to mind the ways authoritarian societies can limit access to knowledge and, in doing so, restrict individual autonomy. The newspaper becomes more than a material or source image; it carries questions of information, censorship, power and who is allowed access to knowledge. Gaelen Pinnock’s work began speaking to Lungisa Qwanta’s in ways that became clearer the longer I lived with the images.

Other pairings came almost instinctively. I could not resist placing Yonela Makoba’s teabag work in conversation with Zaneaca Singh’s sugar works. Tea and sugar are so intimately linked to comfort, hospitality and everyday ritual, yet both are deeply entangled with colonial trade, extraction and systems whose consequences continue to be felt today. Atang Tshikare and Lyndi Sales were another pairing that became exciting to me. Their works open onto connections between cosmology, science, plants, natural systems and forms of knowledge that move between the earthly and the speculative. I placed the work of Chris Soal in conversation with Hanien Conradie’s work. Soal found the bottle caps he uses in the streets of Johannesburg, while Conradie gathered her materials from riverbanks and plants. I was interested in that contrast between the inorganic and the organic – two artists collecting from their immediate environments but encountering very different traces of place. One gathers the discarded remnants of an urban and consumer landscape; the other works with materials embedded in natural systems. I also put Sahlah Davids and Jeanne Gaigher in the same room. Both had been working abstractly and, for works made specifically for this exhibition, began experimenting with figuration. I loved that parallel: two artists independently shifting their visual languages and then finding themselves in conversation within the exhibition.

There are many more connections, and they became central to the curatorial process. One work would lead me to another, sometimes through material, sometimes through process, and sometimes through a shared political or emotional concern. The exhibition gradually became a web of relationships rather than a series of isolated objects. At one stage I considered making the exhibition entirely South African. There was certainly enough work to do that. But ultimately, it felt too restrictive, partly because of the political moment we are living through, when xenophobia and increasingly narrow ideas about nationality and belonging remain so present, but also because this kind of material experimentation is something I have noticed strongly across the African continent.

The final selection was never simply about finding unusual materials. I was interested in artists for whom material is fundamental to the meaning of the work – where you could not simply substitute one material for another without changing what the artwork is saying. That is also why I am drawn to thematic exhibitions. They allow artists across race, gender, age, generation, geography, medium and levels of recognition to enter into a shared conversation. Their differences are not erased, but neither are they confined to fixed categories. Instead, the question becomes: what might very different artists contribute to the same conversation? I am always interested in creating encounters between works that might otherwise never occupy the same room. At the same time, I do not want to explain every connection. Some relationships are quite deliberate, and others emerged unexpectedly, and I hope audiences discover many of them for themselves. A viewer may make a connection that I did not anticipate at all, and that is part of what makes an exhibition alive. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

Material can carry histories of place, labour, culture and exchange. How does the exhibition explore meaning gathered through use, movement and transformation?

Many of the materials in ‘Matereality V2’ have already had lives before they enter the museum. They have circulated through homes, industries, communities, ceremonies, economies or systems of trade and consumption. Through cutting, stitching, weaving, assembling, burning, layering, binding or repetition, those meanings can shift again. Something disposable can become precious. An ordinary domestic material can become political. An industrial product can suddenly speak about the body, land, memory or belonging. As the exhibition developed, I found myself returning to Jane Bennett’s idea of “vibrant matter”. Bennett asks us to reconsider the assumption that matter is passive – that human beings act upon materials and materials obediently receive that action. Instead, she encourages us to think of materials as having their own properties, behaviours and capacities. That became very useful to me while thinking through ‘Matereality’, because artists do not always completely control their materials. Materials sag, crack, stretch, absorb, rust, decay, reflect and resist. Sometimes the artist is working with the material rather than simply imposing something upon it. So you cannot really separate material, process and meaning in many of these works. Very often, the material itself helps to produce that meaning. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

What role does experimentation play in the exhibition, especially in how artists encounter, manipulate or reconsider their materials?

Experimentation is everything. I am constantly fascinated by the ability of artists to look at a material that most of us might overlook and imagine an entirely different function, language or aesthetic for it. There is often an enormous amount of testing, intuition and problem-solving involved: discovering how far something will stretch, what happens when it is heated, cut, stitched, compressed, layered, woven or combined with another material. Sometimes the material refuses to behave as the artist imagined. That resistance is important. There can be a negotiation between artist and material. Materials have characteristics and limitations of their own. They can buckle, unravel, stain, rust, fade, harden, break down or change over time. I think that curiosity is one of the great pleasures of ‘Materiality ’. The exhibition repeatedly asks a very simple question: what else can this thing become? And very often the answer is something completely unexpected. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

How does ‘Matereality V2’ invite audiences to think about the relationship between an artwork’s physical qualities and the ideas or experiences it communicates?

I hope people first encounter the works physically. Before reading a wall text or knowing the story, there is texture, scale, weight, fragility, repetition, colour, density and surface. You might immediately wonder what something is made from, how it was constructed, or even what it might feel like to touch. Then, when you understand why that particular material has been used, the artwork can shift completely. A material that initially appears seductive might carry a difficult history. Something apparently cheap or disposable might involve extraordinary labour. Something visually delicate may come from an industrial or violent process. That relationship between the sensory and the conceptual is central to the exhibition. Sometimes the conversation between two works only becomes apparent when you stand between them. A material used in one work might change the way you understand another. A shared concern with home, violence, memory, science, comfort or colonial history may surface even where the artists are working in completely different ways. For me, that is one of the pleasures of a thematic exhibition. Meaning does not only exist within individual works; it can also happen in the space between them. And I hope viewers find links that I have missed entirely. I also think this physical encounter has particular resonance now. So much of our experience of art – and of the world generally – happens through screens. We scroll past images incredibly quickly. These works ask for another kind of attention. The exhibition asks us not only to look at what an artwork represents, but to consider what it is physically made from, what that material has already experienced, and what the artist has asked it to become. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

The exhibition brings different artistic approaches into conversation within a museum context. How did Iziko’s spaces and collections shape your curatorial thinking?

Working within Iziko inevitably means thinking about history, because the museum contains layers of collecting, classification and ideas about what kinds of artworks and materials have historically been considered worthy of entering a national collection. That becomes particularly interesting with an exhibition such as ‘Matereality’, because many of the artists work with practices or materials historically associated with craft, domestic labour, informal economies or everyday life rather than so-called “fine art”. This second iteration places a stronger emphasis on textile practices, Afro-centric perspectives and indigenous knowledge systems. I am particularly interested in the way practices such as weaving, stitching, beadwork and other forms of hand-making hold knowledge. Historically, many of these practices were separated from “fine art” and placed into categories such as craft, decoration or domestic production. But they contain sophisticated systems of knowledge, memory and transmission. Many contemporary artists are actively drawing upon, disrupting or transforming those traditions. This connects to why thematic exhibitions are so useful within a museum context. I can only speak from my own position as a curator, and I would never claim that an individual exhibition can resolve the much larger structural contradictions within museums or art history. But exhibitions remain one of the most immediate and practical tools available to me. They allow me to work across some of the divisions through which art history and museum collections have traditionally been organised.

There is also a practical institutional reality behind this. When budgets and procedures for growing collections are very limited, exhibitions become another way of bringing artistic voices into the museum, even when we are not yet in a position to acquire those works. They allow us to broaden the conversation, introduce artists who may be absent from the permanent collection and test new relationships between historical holdings and contemporary practice. There is another contradiction that ‘Matereality’ brings into focus too. Museums are designed to preserve things. We try to prevent objects from changing. But many contemporary artists deliberately work with materials that change. They fade. Rust. Break down. Become brittle. Decay. So these works raise fascinating questions about what a museum actually preserves. Is it the original material? The artist’s intention? The process? Can components eventually be replaced? At what point does replacing something fundamentally alter the artwork? That tension is increasingly important for contemporary collections: the museum seeks permanence, while matter itself is often impermanent.

How do questions of place and contemporary life in South Africa enter the exhibition through the artists’ materials, processes and perspectives?

They enter organically because materials are deeply connected to place. Artists work with what surrounds them – culturally, economically, environmentally and politically. Within South Africa, materials can carry extraordinarily complicated histories. They can speak about mining and extraction, land and displacement, migrant labour, clothing and identity, domestic work, inequality, environmental degradation, spirituality, indigenous knowledge systems and histories of making. But I did not want those themes to become neat categories. I did not want textiles in one room, plastic in another and found objects somewhere else. The interesting part is precisely how these histories and materials become entangled. At the same time, I did not want the exhibition to imply that South African artists are somehow only responding to South African concerns. These practices are connected to much larger questions around climate change, consumption, migration, technology, sustainability and belonging. That is one reason the exhibition extends beyond South Africa to selected artists elsewhere on the continent. There is extraordinary material experimentation happening across Africa, often using objects or substances that are locally specific while simultaneously speaking to global systems and concerns. What interests me is precisely that movement between the local and the universal. A material might have a highly specific social history in Cape Town, Johannesburg, Accra, or Harare, but the artwork can simultaneously open onto a much broader conversation about contemporary life. Installation view of exhibition ‘Matereality V2’ , 2026, at Iziko South African National Gallery. Image Courtesy of Gallery.

What questions do you hope ‘Matereality V2’ leaves open about the materials around us and how we understand their histories, possibilities and value?

I hope people leave the exhibition looking at ordinary materials differently. We live surrounded by objects and substances whose histories we rarely think about: where they came from, who made them, what labour was involved, what systems of trade or extraction produced them, what environmental cost they carry, and where they will eventually end up. Artists are particularly good at disrupting that familiarity. They can take something we think we understand and make it strange again. Questions of value are crucial here. Why is one material considered precious and another disposable? Why are certain forms of making described as art while others have historically been classified as craft, domestic labour or decoration? Who decides what is worthy of preservation? I also hope people leave thinking about the relationships between the works. I have spent years carrying these images around, mentally and quite literally, and gradually seeing connections between artists who may never have imagined themselves alongside one another. But once the exhibition opens, those relationships no longer belong only to me. A visitor may see an entirely different connection between two works – through a material, a memory, a colour, a history or an experience. I like the idea that the exhibition can keep generating conversations beyond the ones I consciously constructed. So perhaps it leaves visitors with fairly simple questions: what histories are contained within the objects we encounter every day? Whose labour is embedded within them? Why do we value some things and discard others? What happens when the same material can signify comfort and violence, familiarity and exploitation, intimacy and enormous global systems at the same time? And what possibilities might exist in a material once we stop seeing it only in terms of its intended function? Of course, exhibitions centred on materiality are incredibly common, and artists have been investigating material for centuries. I am certainly not suggesting that ‘Matereality’ introduces something entirely new. My hope is rather to pull together some of the many threads running through contemporary practice – labour, ecology, indigenous knowledge, craft, memory, technology, consumption and value – and see what becomes visible when they are considered together.

In that sense, ‘Matereality V2’ is perhaps an opportunity to take stock: a kind of summary of what I have been noticing over the past several years, and of the extraordinarily inventive ways in which emerging and established artists are making material inseparable from meaning. What I hope it offers is another chapter in that much longer conversation. And perhaps it encourages us to pay closer attention to the things around us – to what materials already contain, to the labour and histories embedded within them, and to what happens when an artist takes something familiar and allows us to see it completely differently.

This exhibition is on view at the Iziko South African National Gallery in Cape Town until 30th June 2027.

"我希望人们离开展览会看平凡的材料不同。我们生活围绕着物品和物质,其故事我们很少想到:他们从哪里来,谁创造了它们,什么劳动参与了,什么贸易或挖掘系统生产了它们,什么环境成本他们承担,最终他们将到哪里结束。艺术家特别好打破这种熟悉。他们可以采取我们认为我们理解的东西,并使它又奇怪。某些形式的制作被描述为艺术,而其他人历史上被归类为工艺,家庭劳动或装饰?谁决定什么值得保存?我也希望人们离开思考作品之间的关系。我已经花了几年携带这些图像周围,精神和相当字面,并逐渐看到艺术家之间的联系,谁可能从未想象自己在彼此旁边。但一旦展览开幕,这些关系不再属于我。通过材料、记忆、颜色、历史或经验,我喜欢这个想法,展览可以继续产生超越我有意识地构建的对话,所以也许它会让参观者提出一个相当简单的问题:我们每天遇到的物体中包含哪些故事?在这些物体中包含哪些工作?为什么我们珍惜某些东西,而不珍惜其他东西?当同样的物质能够同时表达舒适和暴力、熟悉和剥削、亲密和巨大的全球系统时,会发生什么?当然,以物质为中心的展览是非常常见的,艺术家们已经研究物质了几个世纪,我肯定不建议“物质”引入了一些全新的东西,我的希望更能把一些通过当代实践运行的许多线条 - 劳动,生态学,原住民知识,工艺,记忆,技术,消费和价值 - 聚集在一起,看看它们在一起考虑时会看到什么。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这个意义上,“物质性V2”肯定是一个机会来记住:我已经注意到的一种总结,在过去的几年里,以及出现和建立的艺术家正在使材料不可分割的意义的非凡发明方式。我希望它提供的是这个更长的对话的另一个章节。让我们完全不同地看待它。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该展览在开普敦的伊齐科南非国家画廊上展开,直到2027年6月30日。", "links": [{"text": "Iziko South African National Gallery", "url": "https://www.iziko.org.za/exhibitions/matereality-v2/"}], "translated": true}]
